speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head J of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Charter of the United Nations enshrines the prohibition against the use of force – except in self-defence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This rule is generally regarded as jus cogens – or a peremptory norm of international law – which means it is a rule that permits for no derogation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Russia is a member of the Security Council of the United Nations (UN) – the body that is supposed to lead the collective response of the UN to uphold international law.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: When the rule of international law is threatened or breaks down, it leaves small nations like us particularly vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Non-state actors are also becoming more powerful and potentially destabilising.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is a conflict between Israel, which is – some argue – an occupying power in the Gaza; and Hamas, an organisation that has de facto control over the territory, but as a non-state actor.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The violence has spread beyond the Gaza Strip, spilling into Lebanon and the Red Sea – threatening to destabilise the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The world is likely be more volatile and unpredictable in the coming year.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As a small country, Singapore is vulnerable to changes in its external security environment – a peaceful order is critical to Singapore's success.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Could the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) therefore provide an update on the major global and regional trends that MINDEF and the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) are closely monitoring, and how MINDEF and SAF will be affected by these trends?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, in the last few years, we stood witness to the winds of change sweeping across our globe.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The pillars of international order have trembled and weakened under the weight of discord and conflict – casting shadows of uncertainty on all of us.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Let us take for a moment to reflect on the sobering reality that the Russia-Ukraine War, is now into its third year.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It has transcended mere territorial battlegrounds and has spilled into the virtual realm of cyber warfare and disinformation – shaping perceptions and narratives everywhere.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Ukraine's resilient defence, buoyed by initial international solidarity – albeit now more tenuous than it was at the start of the war – stands as a testament to the indomitable spirit of the Ukrainian people.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, regrettably, the horizon remains shrouded in ambiguity – devoid of a clear end to this protracted conflict.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And while the world's gaze was on Europe, another conflict rages now in the Middle East, where the ancient sands bear witness to a modern-day tragedy unfolding before all of us.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The clash between Israel and Hamas serves as a poignant reminder of unresolved grievances and deep-seated animosities that have marred the region not just for decades – but for centuries and millennia.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The hopes for a lasting peace seem now dashed against the rocks of historical enmity, leaving the world grappling for solutions in the face of entrenched divisions – not just far from our shores but within our own borders and between communities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this crucible of conflict, we witness the evolution of warfare itself, where traditional boundaries between conventional and unconventional tactics now blur into obscurity.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Tactical innovation have birthed a new breed of weaponry, where hybrid tools serve as the vanguards of destruction in an ever-shifting landscape of battle.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Amidst this chaos and turmoil that grip our world, we must not lose sight of the implications that they hold for all of us – especially here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore, despite our small size, stands as a beacon of stability in a turbulent sea and it is incumbent upon us to remain vigilant, adaptable and resolute in the defence of our sovereignty.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As we navigate the treacherous waters, let us stand firm against the tides of adversity – fortified by the knowledge that together, we can overcome even the greatest of challenges.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Chairman, the world is unfortunately experiencing more political turbulence and military strife.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have witnessed two major conflicts in the last few years and despite many international appeasement attempts, there are no signs of abatement.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The rising temperature of US-China relations further adds to the global woes.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Wary of the implications and the undercurrents of all these discords, many governments have increased their defence spending and some have gone on defence shopping sprees to fill their capability gaps.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In Singapore's case, we have always put national defence as our priority.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It has always been a non-negotiable since our Independence.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In spite of the trade-offs and opportunity cost, our Government – with the trust and confidence of our citizens – has made steady investments in defence, as we have understood the importance of self-reliance.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is in this light that I would like to ask the Minister for Defence about our defence expenditure.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What are the main issues or challenges in the process of procurement and maintenance and how is the Ministry overcoming these constraints?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Chairman, as my Parliamentary colleagues have said, it has been over two years since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As Ukraine faces mounting shortages in traditional weapons systems and ammunition, their military has had to deploy low-cost drones on an improvised basis – which they have done with considerable success.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This is not the first conflict where unmanned aerial vehicles are being deployed in significant numbers, but the scale at which the drones have been deployed has resulted in major changes to the warfighting on the battlefield.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In fact, the unprecedented numbers have led some to call this the world's first drone war.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Apart from electronic-warfare drone swarms, we are also seeing the use of cyber warfare not just to target civilian infrastructure but also to achieve battlefield intelligence dominance in the Israel-Hamas conflict.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In the Red Sea crisis, the Houthis are weaponising civilian technology to disrupt international trade flow and leveraging asymmetrical warfare by using anti-tank and anti-aircraft missiles.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In the coming years, we can expect that warfare will be further shaped by the use of artificial intelligence and direct-energy weapons.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With technological advances changing the face of warfare so rapidly, how can MINDEF ensure that that the SAF is able to deal with evolving security threats in a timely, but financially prudent manner?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: : Chairman, at last year's COS debate, Defence Minister Dr Ng said to the House that "we must never forget that defence is a long-term business." He went on to elaborate that for the SAF, major systems and platforms take 10 to 15 years to conceptualise, build and integrate into its fighting force, assuming all goes well.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am glad that Singapore has always taken a long-term view on defence.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We cannot wait until conflict is at our doorstep, in order to prepare and defend ourselves.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, governments around the world have been rushing to build and buy new weapons as the war has put a significant strain on their stockpiles.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, even with increased spending in defence, it could be years before countries start to reap the dividends of their increased investment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such are the unfortunate consequences of not making consistent investments in defence.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In March last year, the online publication Defense News reported that Italy was considering the quick procurement of tanks and infantry fighting vehicles to serve as gap fillers before long-term projects took shape.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The war in Ukraine has brought to the fore the importance of ground warfare capabilities, and Italy's stock of tanks and infantry fighting vehicles were ageing and depleting.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope that in Singapore, we take in the hard lessons learnt by other countries.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As the nature of conflict evolves, it is important for Singapore to be able to effectively defend herself against increasingly sophisticated conventional military and non-conventional threats.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In particular, the war in Ukraine has shown us the continued importance of countries maintaining high-end, conventional military capabilities.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would MINDEF provide an update on the progress of the SAF's acquisitions and capability development plans?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, MINDEF had previously announced plans to acquire the F-35B fighter jets.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Can MINDEF provide an update on this acquisition?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: As a small country with no strategic depth, it is important for Singapore to have an effective military to deter potential aggression.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We are keenly aware that it is necessary for us to modernise our military and ensure that the SAF can protect Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Over the past few years, MINDEF has provided updates on the modernisation of the Republic of Singapore Air Force (RSAF) through the purchase of advanced fighter aircraft and other systems, which play a pivotal role in a nation's defence capabilities.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Minister for Defence had also said that the RSAF would take delivery of its first four aircraft in 2026.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, over the past few years, the world seen many supply chain challenges, which have impacted the timelines for the delivery of some military platforms.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, given Singapore's declining birth rates, we can expect that our full-time national servicemen and operationally ready National Servicemen (NSmen) cohorts will shrink in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The SAF will need to do more, with less manpower.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: It is clear that new technologies have the potential to help organisations optimise and streamline operations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Notably, the use of drones and other unmanned technologies can help to make up for tighter manpower constraints, and I understand that MINDEF has already made significant progress in this area.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Unmanned technologies also enhance the military's capability edge.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Mechanised warfare reduces the need to put troops in danger.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: There is also an ability to fight with precision, while limiting human frailties and vulnerabilities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: For this reason, I ask about updates and developments in this area regularly in COS debates.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I am heartened that MINDEF normally reports impressive developments on this front each year.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: During last year's COS debate, the Minister for Defence highlighted that when used at scale, unmanned platforms in the air, land and sea would be a game changer in the future.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: We have seen examples of drones being used in ongoing conflicts, such as in Ukraine and in the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Given the role that unmanned and autonomous technologies will play in the military domain moving forward, it is more important than ever for the SAF to utilise and integrate such technologies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: On the flip side though, automated technologies also pose greater risk to our forces, given barriers to entry and costs are relatively low.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This may provide opportunities for enemies, including non-state actors, to use these technologies to threaten Singapore's securities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Could MINDEF provide an update on how the SAF has been integrating unmanned technologies to enhance its capabilities, and also dealing with the potential threat from these technologies?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Chairman, in January this year, Houthi rebels fired what the Associated Press reported as their "largest-ever barrage of drones and missiles" targeting shipping in the Red Sea.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And just days ago, the US Central Command said that it had observed the Houthis using underwater drones against ships for the first time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is growing commentary on the increasingly consequential role drones will play as a terrorist tactic and in the wars of the future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They can also be deployed at scale and pose a significant threat to our security.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In its attacks on 7 October 2023, Hamas deployed commercial quadcopter drones with explosives to disrupt Israeli military infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In the Ukrainian-Russian war, drones have changed the complex of what was a conventional war.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The attacks have changed because of attack and kamikaze drones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There were reports of commercial drones being retrofitted with explosives to attack conventional armies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Furthermore, there has been greater use of drones for surveillance and to direct artillery fire.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Even the most advanced militaries are still grappling with how best to respond to these threats and new developments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The US' interceptions have proven to be effective.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, one can imagine that the risks to servicemen to perform these missions are significant and the cost of each mission is high.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If adversaries were to scale up such attacks, existing military responses would not be sustainable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have not even examined how a swarm drone attack could be successfully defended, especially when it could be fully autonomous in time to come.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Large swarms of drones can overwhelm conventional defences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This leads to questions on whether current air defences are adequate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The threat that I have described is just one that we are aware of today.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But bad actors are continuing to find even more creative and cost-effective ways to evade and weaken conventional military defences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These tactics could exploit new technologies or commercially available, dual-use platforms.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Chairman, the nature of warfare is evolving, with battles no longer confined to the traditional physical domains of the sea, air and land.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is taking place in the digital domain.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Increasingly, it is possible to inflict more damage by infiltrating networks, sabotaging government or civilian infrastructure and disrupting day-to-day operations.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Similar to conventional warfare, such attacks target a country by eroding trust in the government, undermine social cohesion and weaken military industrial capacity.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We have seen this strategy play out, for example, the hacking operations on Israeli sites and apps, as well as multiple Internet blackouts in the Gaza Strip since the start of the Israeli-Hamas conflict.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Chairman, in a commentary published by the S.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Rajaratnam School of International Studies, Asst Prof Michael Raska wrote that the main source of strategic advantage in the next 10 years will lie in the ability of modern military organisations to fully integrate innovations in artificial intelligence, cyber power and data science, as well as cognitive science and robotics across all levels of operations and warfare.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: For the SAF to maintain its edge, it should continuously evolve to take advantage of new digital technologies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: The SAF should also continuously develop responses to defend against new threats.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: In view of these rapidly evolving developments, I think that the establishment of the SAF's DIS over a year ago was very timely.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: It may take many years to fully integrate various digital and cyber capabilities and assets across all levels of operations, and of course, across the three Services, and for the service personnel to build up operational experience.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: The Ministry is taking the right and necessary steps.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: What steps have been taken to build up its capabilities?

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: How has the DIS been working together with the other agencies in Singapore that operate in the digital domain, in order to boost our security?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, many SAF regulars and NSmen have had the opportunity to train overseas, which allows them to gain ground experience and apply their skills and knowledge in an operational context.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is especially critical for certain types of training that would otherwise be challenging or impossible here, given Singapore's space constraints.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As our global outlook becomes more uncertain, we cannot assume that we will always be able to maintain our current access to overseas training areas.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is, therefore, important to explore different ways to ensure that our NSmen and women train well and remain operationally ready.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can MINDEF provide an update on efforts to improve local and overseas training?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In particular, how are we leveraging technological advancements to maximise the value and efficiency of the SAF's training?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What opportunities has the SAF taken advantage of, to provide our servicemen with practical experiences in either conflict zones or humanitarian missions abroad?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Chairman, my cut is on using technology to improve processes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While the worst of the pandemic might be behind us, it has impacted how we live and work, and pushes us towards embracing new ways of working, specifically going digital and leveraging technologies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: From cloud technology to AI tools to robotic assistance, we have read about how these technologies are transforming the modern workplace.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As the world becomes more digitalised, expectations for greater productivity and efficiency will likely ensue.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We will need to seize the opportunity to lock in the digital gain and deliver better and also faster.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: MINDEF and the SAF has embraced digitalisation and modernised many generations of our forces since decades ago.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, continued investments in our Air Force and Navy, as well as efforts to work with regional and international partners, provide Singapore with an added guarantee of such access.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our nation's interests beneath the waves are no less important.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Submarine cables bring data from everything from our financial markets to design blueprints and overseas orders to and from Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These cables also help connect the Middle East, South Asia, and with us in Southeast and Northeast Asia.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I understand that there are even plans to increase the number of submarine cable landing sites in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are also plans to provide electricity to Singapore via undersea cables.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They come in addition to undersea pipelines to carry gas, including from West Natuna in Indonesia.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These risks are more real, with increased tensions in Asia and the South China Sea, driven by US-PRC competition and growing maritime traffic.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What are the efforts to enhance such capabilities?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, in our rapidly changing world, the nature of threats we face is evolving.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We now on confront a growing array of non-conventional security challenges.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Terrorism, cyber-attacks and the spread of disinformation are on the rise, both in frequency and impact.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just last October, a devastating terrorist attack orchestrated by Hamas struck Israel, claiming the lives of innocent individuals.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This heinous act sparked a brutal conflict between Israel and Hamas.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Israel's disproportionate force and violence, despite the right to self-defence, has led to the loss of thousands of lives and the displacement of countless others.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The repercussions of this conflict extend far beyond their immediate battlegrounds.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Furthermore, cyber-attacks and the dissemination of false information have become preferred tactics for hostile entities seeking to further their agendas.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These attacks are insidious, widespread and challenging to trace, capable of inflicting severe damage on our critical infrastructure and undermining public trust.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Given Singapore's heavy reliance on digital technologies, we must remain vigilant against such threats.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Take, for example, the issue of ransomware, which remains a serious concern in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is clear therefore the challenges cannot be tackled by any single nation alone.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, I am eager to learn about the strategies and initiatives undertaken by MINDEF to address these common threats that transcend our national borders.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This initiative is crucial because cyber and information threats are multifaceted and constantly evolving.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is clear that collaboration with other ASEAN member states and international partners is essential.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, I am also keen to find out from the Minister for Defence about the progress of ACICE and its plans for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Chairman, Mr Vikram Nair began his cut by asserting that our world is a much more dangerous world.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Subsequent Members of Parliament (MPs) gave their spiels on the events around us.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I do not think anyone in this House or out of it needs to be convinced that indeed the world has become a more dangerous place.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We are all concerned that the US and China can clash over Taiwan.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If that happens, that will be a very bleak Asia for a very long time.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: When was this region beset with such trouble?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If you remember your Shakespeare: "double, double toil and trouble; fire burn and cauldron bubble".

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The last time the region experienced this kind of turmoil and potential danger was probably in the 1980s during the Sino-Viet Conflicts that lasted from 1979 to 1991.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Singapore's Pioneer Generation (PG) lived through those tumultuous, perilous times, not only through that period, but for 60 years.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Japanese Occupation in the 1940s, the Korean War, the Vietnam War, Konfrontasi. 60 years.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew recounted that he had to sing four national anthems because of the political upheavals that lasted 60 years.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Those experiences hardened the PG that were born in the 1920s and 1930s.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And the first order of the day when we gained Independence was to form the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF).

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: My generation and for some of us in this House, were born in the 1950s and 1960s, the Merdeka Generation (MG).

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Many families like mine were poor at the start, but as Singapore prospered, so did we.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It was the heyday for open trade and liberalisation, and when the Cold War ended in 1991, the global economy took off, lifting standards of living even higher today.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, Singapore's per capita gross domestic product (GDP) is the highest in Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: When did we exceed Japan, the second highest?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: With a strong dollar, overseas travel has become less expensive.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I still remember as a boy when £1 was more than S$7.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Now, hordes of Singaporeans go to Japan – not quite expensive.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Sixty years of confrontation the PG lived through.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The MG has lived through 30 years of relative peace.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And we have assumed that this is the norm.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Which is the norm – what the PG went through, or what the MG went through?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If you had asked me even five years ago, I would have said that the current generation – they are lumped together, Gen X, Millennials, Gen Z and other alphabets – would be just as lucky as the MG.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Because despite Brexit, the European Union (EU) held – if you remember, the EU was formed in 1993.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: During that time, there was a rising economic co-dependency with Russia, even in energy supplies.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: You do not buy gas in that proportion, if you did not believe in peace and lasting peace.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Russia's invasion of Ukraine dealt a death blow to Europe's integration for a generation at least.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Worse still, seeds of future discord and conflict have been sown.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs, Josep Borrell said at the Shangri-La Dialogue held here last year, "This war is changing the role of Europe.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Europe was and is a project for peace and about peace.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But now we face a world where war is something that is in every corner, and these corners are close to our houses." In the Middle East, the signed Abraham Accords held out the future of accelerated peace and progress in that region.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The zeitgeist following the Abraham Accords, not seen or thought possible for a long time, was to avoid conflict and find common cause so that that region could develop economically.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This was a dictum following Deng Xiaoping: "to get rich is glorious", instead of war.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And for this higher cause, even Saudi Arabia's Mohammed bin Salman reversed his position with the Houthis in Yemen, whom he had unleashed deadly strikes on earlier on.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, in this conflict, there is a reversal of roles.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The plan on the US side is to conscribe it to limited areas, particularly high-end technology that have a bearing on national security.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In theory, this seems possible. "Small yard, high fences" is the neat way that the US puts it.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But in practice, it is much harder because in the name of national security, the yard could get bigger.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Right now, a bill in the US Congress targets to exclude Chinese biopharma manufacturing because, I suppose, you could produce something, pharmaceuticals, that weakens your national security.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And of course, there is capital, the most fungible of all assets.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If a country or company invests large sums in China, would it be seen as helping the potential adversary?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And if so, what punitive measures or restrictions might be taken against that country?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In this inter-connected world, will borders erected for national security regress the world to alliances and trade blocs as it did pre-World Wars I and II, and the Cold War?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We are seeing this before our very eyes.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We are seeing it play out: all the world's a stage.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It will take one, two decades for these various scenarios to come to fruition, whatever the outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Two weeks ago, I was at the Munich Security Conference, the 60th.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They titled this 60th Munich Security Conference as "Lose-Lose?" because everywhere they turned, and they analysed all the situations, every scenario they had talked about, both sides lose, and the world loses.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In 2014, I attended the 50th Munich Security Conference.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: On stage was Henry Kissinger, Helmut Schmidt, former French President Valéry Giscard d'Estaing.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It has been the 50th Munich Security Conference.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Helmut Schmidt and Henry Kissinger had been present in the inaugural Munich Security Conference in 1963.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I remember President Valéry Giscard d'Estaing saying that Europe had eliminated the concept of war.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I can assure this House that surprises and unintended consequences are in store, some linked, others completely out of the blue.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: When the ambient temperature of geopolitics rises, sparks and fires will arise from multiple sources.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, I have reversed my assessment for today's generation in Singapore and elsewhere.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is imponderable and your guess is as good as mine.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But the most important question, I think, is what some Members here have said – Vikram Nair, Alex Yam and others.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: What can Singapore, as a small country, and Singaporeans, do realistically to prepare ourselves as best as we can for disruptions and unintended consequences?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Because there will be disruptions and intended consequences – that we can be sure.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: How we meet it, we are not sure.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I remember US Defense Secretary Gates; I quote him often for this quote.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: He was addressing West Point Military Academy graduates.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And he told the West Point graduates that for the last decade, the US Department of Defense's record for predicting where they would be within a year of the conflict, was perfect.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: One year, with all its machinery of intelligence collection and prediction, the US Administration never got it right.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, we cannot pretend to know what will come and yet, we have to prepare.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, how do we prepare Singapore for this uncertain future?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: First, I think, we should recognise that Singaporeans have more to protect and with more resources to do so, compared to the PG and MG.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Some Singaporeans may remember the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq in 1990.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Among the justifications for the invasion, Iraq accused Kuwait of stealing oil – there was a particular field, it is called Al-Rumaylah oil field, which straddles both states, across the borders.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Iraq said, "you are pumping from your side, but you are siphoning off from my side." Geographically, I think it is possible, but that was the claim, anyhow.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Wealthy, small Kuwait with its rich resources was a tempting and lucrative victim.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Wealthy, small Singapore can be a lucrative target, without a strong defence.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In that invasion, the US came to the rescue of Kuwait and led 42 countries to join forces in an air and ground war.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: A strong SAF acts a deterrent against aggression towards us and keeps adventurism at bay.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: When I listen to the speeches of MPs, it was heartening because all of you understand, across the aisle, of whatever political persuasion, we are on our own.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And I want to thank Members of this House for supporting MINDEF's Budget every year.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We do spend precious dollars consistently on defence, as some of you observed.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Money which could have benefited other causes, but we know that without security, there can be no progress.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Singapore was ranked the sixth most peaceful country in the world in the latest Global Peace Index.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I do not know and do not want to find out, what our ranking would have been if we had not put in the necessary investments to build a strong SAF.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I think that experiment would be too costly.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong asked to give us details on the defence spending this year and subsequent years.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If you compare this to 2022, the increase is higher, but that was because we were catching up – projects and activities disrupted by the pandemic.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These handouts are instructive, so, while you are listening, take your time to peruse it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You can also access this through SG PARL MP mobile app.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: By the way, every time Budget comes around, I pick up and compare figures.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The average Middle East spending, Middle Eastern countries is about 4% of GDP.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Europe, of course, is undergoing huge turmoil, they have not spent even 2%.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But two decades ago, we were spending 5% of GDP on defence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Alex Yam, Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Don Wee asked "That is the overall picture, but where has this spending gone?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And how are you preparing the SAF?" These are excellent questions.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is also not because our manpower has come down.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think Mr Vikram noted that our NS cohorts, he said, "will be coming down." I must tell him it has already come down.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And the last time we were in a dragon year, all of us expected that to have good news.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We never had real dragons for a long time since 1988.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Beyond that, every dragon cycle are mini dragons.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I hope we are proven wrong this year, but let us leave that to another Ministry.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It has come down because as various Defence Ministers and including MPs have said, we sustained defence spending and that was the most effective and efficient means of building a strong military over the longer term.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, today, we are reaping dividends of the sums we put in steadily over the past 20 years.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And if we continue to invest wisely, we will reap more dividends in the future.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If you read the newspapers today, what the Denmark, either the Defence Minister or Prime Minister was saying, "we should cut back on welfare to increase our defence spending." We never want to be in that position.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Steady long-term defence spending enables platforms and capabilities to mature over the necessary timeline and to enhance synergy and reap efficiencies.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Ms Poh Li San asked about our F-35s.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, that is a good place to start, to illustrate what I mean.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The F-35s when operational will put the RSAF in the Premier League.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The sixth generations are being developed, but it will take some time.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, when they are operational, we will be in the Premier League.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: When did we start looking at the F-35 programme?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You think it is a matter of course, right?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But we are in a very, very different position.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We are in Singapore – 5.5 million people, looking at F-35s.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And we started evaluating the F-35s in 2004, 20 years ago.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: First, as a Security Cooperation Participant, and then we dipped our feet in the water tentatively, ordered four aircrafts for evaluation.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But since then, as Ms Poh Li San recognised, events have overtaken that.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Because since that period, the F-35s have been deployed by other air forces for real missions, which is the final test of any evaluation, final test of any combat platform.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, for example, the US and the UK, their F-35s, they conducted successful strikes against ISIS in the Middle East.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: More recently, the US used their F-35s to locate and identify surface-to-air missile sites of Russian units in Ukraine.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, to-date, more than 900 F-35s have flown in operations around the world.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: When we began our evaluation, these were not the numbers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And their battlefield successes have prompted more countries – Switzerland, Germany, to jump on board the F-35 programme.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Other countries, South Korea, Japan, UK, have placed additional orders.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, a question was asked whether there are supply chain disruptions?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Not for the F-35, in fact, the reverse.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: More orders have gone in because around the world, they have recognised that the F-35 is a proven fifth generation fighter aircraft; advanced sense and strike capabilities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, globally, there are close to 2,500 F-35s, and that is a healthy pipeline on the order book.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Because of that the price is now more competitive.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In fact, if you buy an F-35, put in an order for it, it is not like a car, but you understand what I am saying.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If you put in an order for an F-35 today, the price is comparable to an F-15EX.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, we will capitalise on this window of opportunity to accelerate our F-35 programme.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The RSAF could take these decisions deliberately, cool and calculated mindset, because of the steady defence spending over the years.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And this allowed our mid-life upgrade of F-16Cs, our Ds and D+s, which the F-35 will replace.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And the subsequent eight F-35Bs that we are in 2028.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That is a couple of years from now.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have to deprioritise other projects for this opportunity buy, but we have done our calculations and we think that this is the best time to put in the order for the F-35As.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Because the F-35As are designed for greater endurance.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They have the ability to carry a payload at higher capacity.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They complement the F-35Bs which are short, take off and vertical landing, because the F-35As are bigger, bulkier, bigger range, and provide more operational flexibility.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Capable of performing the full suite of missions required to defend Singapore skies.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This will be a capable Air Force above all to protect our skies.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For the Navy, our first invincible class submarine returned to Singapore last year.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If you notice, then it is not doing its job.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Submarines are a hefty investment and obviously, I cannot use them for National Day Parade, like I do our planes.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But rest assured that our submarines will silently and stealthily protect the waters around us.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Later this year, we will commission her, as well as launch the fourth and final submarine in Kiel.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This submarine programme, custom made for the RSN – this is the first time we have got them custom-made.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Previously, we ordered used submarines, adapted for our use, of course.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But this is the first time, from scratch, we dealt with the defence supplier, this is what we need.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And as some of you rightly pointed out, including Mr Don Wee, you cannot decide that you are going to have defences up.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: President Zelensky spoke at the recent Munich Security Conference, in person.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He sent a chill down the audience's spine, when he said, I think, "You European countries, are not ready for an invasion!" Ukraine, despite all its preparations, was not ready.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For the next few days, that was the question back and forth, "Are we ready for an invasion?" So, if you look The Economist's front page, the title is: Is Europe Ready?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Because they have not committed to that defence spending.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Questions were asked, what happens if the US – they are looking at elections, too – what happens if the US reduces its commitment?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And only now are the Europeans saying we have to be responsible for our own defence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Those of you who are military buffs will understand what I mean.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For the Army, the next-generation Armoured Tracked Carriers (ATCs) and the next-generation Howitzers will be brought into service.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The ATCs will operate alongside the Bronco Tracked Carrier and replace the older BV206.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Some of you may have used it – more protected, more mobile.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I know that some Members here are from the artillery and will appreciate the difference between the new Howitzer and the old field Howitzer 2000 that they operated.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You have memories of your old Howitzer that you operated.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Vikram Nair and Mr Henry Kwek asked what about unmanned capabilities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Ukraine situation, the situation in the Middle East, have proven that unmanned platforms are already part of today's current war, not even future.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In other words, no person on it, fully unmanned, automated.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It will patrol the Singapore Strait alongside our Littoral Mission Vessels and patrol vessels.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Locally designed, manufactured, these USVs, fully autonomous, can navigate our busy shipping lanes.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Touch wood, that is what they promised me.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is a busy shipping strait, and these are unmanned, but I think they were put to trials and they performed.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In addition, our Navy ships will have Close-Range Unmanned Aerial Vehicles by the second half of this year to extend their range for surveillance.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The UAVs will also filter down to the soldiers in the Army.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Some of you are sci-fi buffs and you know the movies where you have your own personal android that follows you that can survey and shoot people and protect you.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We are not there yet, but our Army soldiers can use their own micro-UAVs.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They will be an asset for soldiers on foot for last-mile surveillance.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And we are tapping on a new generation of NSmen who are tech-savvy.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He comes from 3rd Battalion Singapore Infantry Regiment (3 SIR) to refine the drone tactics, techniques, procedures, including launching and operating from a Terrex.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And we will continue to harness the skills of our NSmen to strengthen our capabilities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Vikram Nair asked if we can use it, and they gave examples of current missions in Ukraine, in the Middle East, others can use it against us.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You have to assume that a potential aggressor can do the same.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Terrorists can use low-cost drones to launch attacks here.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It makes very little sense to launch a couple of million-door missiles to attack a couple of thousand dollars drone.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We set up groups to brainstorm and develop sustainable countermeasures.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And they include off-the-shelf solutions: jammer guns, or our usual rifles fitted with a smart fire control system, an on-board computer to accurately shoot down a small drone.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Shawn Huang and Mr Don Wee said that the digital domain is an increasingly contested battleground.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And that was the reason we formed the DIS in 2022, to build up competencies, to work closely with other national agencies.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We had about 200 frontline cyber defenders, 25 other national agencies.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Scenarios simulated attacks by both ransomware, some of you talked about it, and nation-state cyber attackers on our key infrastructure: power, water, 5G telecommunications.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, in other words, you sit them in a room, you simulate the attacks, how do we defend?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This exercise will be like their live firing, will be held regularly to expand and cover more sectors.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We are building a digital range because you cannot do it on live systems, right?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It will allow us to scale, add complexity and realism in this digital domain.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: All in all, when it concerns hardware and systems for SAF, our steady defence spending has built up an SAF that is modernised and effective with a full suite of capabilities against threats: air, land, sea and cyberspace.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is a short summary statement and it belies the decades of hard work and commitment by our servicemen and women, including some in the House, and your constant support for MINDEF's budget.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I have shown Members what it looks like in the ORBAT in the handout, but we must never forget people.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We are only as good as our people, no matter how advanced our platforms.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And we have made sizeable investments in building up infrastructure to train our NSmen and Regulars.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, if you look at the handout, SAFTI City Phase 1, together with our three Instrumented Battle Circuits.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: During my time, some of you maybe also, when you do exercises, you use blanks and bang, bang, bang, bang.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, I pretend to shoot you, you pretend to shoot back and nobody dies.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Well, we have come a long way from that.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Now, it is transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), which are electronic RFID things.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If your vehicle is shot, it does not move.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have built that up, but for urban built-up areas, we do not have that.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That is what SAFTI City Phase 1 will do.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Instrumented Battle Circuits means you go into a building, in a room, it is the same outfit, and if you are shot, you are shot.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, it is very good training because you can do an after-action review (AAR), video playback, see what you have done wrong.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It was the largest-ever edition of Exercise Wallaby.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Then, there is the adjacent Greenvale Training Area.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We can deploy up to 14,000 personnel, 2,400 vehicles and equipment annually.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We will have improved administrative medical facilities by 2024.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This took years to build up, but it is coming to fruition.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have been training in the Shoalwater Bay training area since 1990, and I want to thank, on our behalf, the government and the people of Australia for these opportunities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I have tried to give various examples to see where our defence dollars have gone over the years, and the overall picture is one of continuous progress and virtuous cycle, spiralling up even when new threats arise.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But it is about the mindset among MINDEF and SAF personnel, the way we approach challenges, the constant emphasis to do things better, safer, not only to protect Singapore, but to improve the lived experience of our soldiers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Patrick Tay said this is "digital gain", and I agree with him.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, we are using smarter chatbots to answer HR enquiries so that you do not have to go back and forth.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For some restricted areas in MINDEF HQ, facial recognition is the norm to control access.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If you are a foreign person, it shoots you.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I am just trying to see if you are still awake.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It just recognises you, and if it does not, you cannot go in.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: DSTA employees no longer require a camp pass to go to work because of this technology.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The 2nd People's Defence Force (2PDF) is in the process of operationalising facial recognition for camp access.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The aim is to progressively roll this out to the rest of our camps and bases to be the norm during peacetime.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: During war and periods of tension (POT), I think there may be issues.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The applications of AI, when we apply it, but we have to do it judiciously.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You will see in your handout, the new Central Manpower Base (CMPB) opposite Cashew MRT.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I am not sure who else; some of us in that vintage, we were none the wiser 18-year-olds.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You go to Dempsey, and after that you go to General Equipment Base (GEB).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Some of you grew up in the era of Depot Road.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Well, the new CMPB is opposite Cashew MRT.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think this will be probably the permanent home.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: At the outset, I posed this question: what can Singapore do to secure our future in a turbulent world?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The answer is mundane but never simple – build a strong SAF for deterrence, but even that is not enough.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We commemorate the 40th anniversary of Total Defence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong launched the Exercise SG Ready.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Members may have participated and Senior Minister of State Zaqy will speak more on this.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I also said that we must not expect another country to come to rescue us like Kuwait.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But that certainly does not mean we do not work with like-minded countries.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is what Members are talking about, to deal with transnational issues, Mr Alex Yam and Ms Sylvia Lim.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I agree completely with Ms Lim that we have critical underwater infrastructure, subsea cables and pipelines.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Because in 2019, ASEAN developed guidelines for strengthening the resilience and repair of telecommunications submarine cables.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) sets an international legal framework to govern underwater critical infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Singapore works with partners to protect this infrastructure because we are either the intermediary or the tail end, and we are a hub for fibre optics subsea cables, including more subsea cables.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But, in truth, it is thousands and thousands of miles of, whether it is gas pipelines, subsea cables.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If they are sabotaged, there will be disruption.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Certain militaries have now commissioned ships to map the entire universe, meaning subsea cables all around the world.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But all you need is to disrupt one point far away, and the whole so-called supply chain is disrupted.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have some redundancy because we have more than one fibre optic subsea cable.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The natural gas pipelines of Singapore are designed and built to international standards.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, within our waters, they are protected with rock armour and laid in no-anchor zones.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For redundancy, we have the capacity to import liquefied natural gas (LNG) to meet our electricity needs.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Terrorism is another prime example, and I think Mr Alex Yam talked about the ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting Cybersecurity and Information Centre of Excellence (ACICE).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is to deal with cyber disinformation and information threats.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And we held our inaugural Digital Defence Symposium and ASEAN Roundtable.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That does not mean all problems can be solved, but we have to build credibility and partnerships.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And lastly, for humanitarian efforts, Mr Zhulkarnain Rahim talked about this – our Changi Regional Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief Coordination Centre was set up in 2014 to better coordinate our efforts with local and international agenices.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Chairman, I want to close, and Senior Minister of State Zaqy and Senior Minister of State Heng will deal with other issues that Members have raised.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But let me again reiterate my deep thanks to the Members of this House.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have not had difficulty passing MINDEF's Budget.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Your questions have not been too hard or too spiky.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And I think it reflects: one, the understanding that we are so vulnerable.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So many examples and, honestly, for the last five years, it has not been difficult to sell defence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We see a turbulent world, but we must remember even in peaceful times; I gave the example of a PG that underwent 60 years of turbulence versus this generation of 30 years of peace – which is the norm.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We may very well revert to the PG – 60 years of turbulence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We do not know what the future will bring but as long as we have a strong SAF, we have some deterrence, protection, and we can determine our own future if our people are united and with a strong SAF and various other agencies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is a well-known fact that Singapore is one of the fastest ageing societies in the world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Despite our best efforts, Singapore's total fertility rate continues to decline.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This means a smaller full-time National Servicemen (NSF) cohort over time.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: At the same time, the nature of warfare has evolved tremendously.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This is also one of Singapore's core strengths, as one of remaining countries that has a conscription service.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As such, can the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) share more about how we are optimising the deployment of our NSmen?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, the sharp escalation of conflict in recent years, including in Europe and the Middle East, have brought the SAF into focus.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The wars being fought today are more complex.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A United States (US) general observed that Ukraine's information and media operations took 17,000 Russians off the battlefield without firing a shot.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Pre-enlistees are assessed on their ability to safely perform the running, jumping and load-bearing that are necessary for specific vocational roles.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Considering our ageing population and declining fertility rates and the creation of new roles like the Digital and Intelligence Service (DIS), are there any updates on the implementation of functional assessments for pre-enlistees?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will they extend beyond physical tests to intellectual tests, for example?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is a good initiative for our young NSFs to learn and be prepared for the workforce while they undergo training to defend Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Through the Work-Learn Scheme, NSFs have the opportunity to put what they have learnt into practice.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In turn, the hands-on knowledge they have gained also enhances their understanding of what they have studied.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This could also help them to better envision their future career pathways, as they would be in a better position to discern if they would like to pursue particular areas of study in the future.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can MINDEF provide an update of the Work-Learn Scheme?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How many have benefitted from this scheme and are there plans for expansion?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my earlier cut, I talked about my support for the Work-Learn Scheme, which provides opportunities for our NSFs to work towards a diploma or university degree while serving in the SAF.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In our polytechnics, we are seeing students developing critical knowledge in fields that have military applications, including engineering and IT.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is synergy between their areas of interest, their studies and what can be applied to SAF's operational needs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As our population grows increasingly well-educated and skilled, our NSmen will also bring to the table a diverse range of talent and experience that could be useful to the SAF.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The NS system should have the necessary structures and processes in place to ensure that we are making the best use of NSmen's expertise.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will become increasingly important as falling fertility rates affect the number of enlistees the SAF takes in each year.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, NS is the bedrock of our national defence, a duty that every generation of NSmen embraces with honour and commitment.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Year after year, our NSmen dedicate – serving, defending and protecting our cherished nation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Given the complexities and challenges this vital service entails, to ensure that our NSmen are comprehensively supported in their roles, we must guarantee their safety during training, ensuring they can prepare for their duties without compromising their well-being.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Achieving this balance between rigorous training and safety is paramount, as it directly impacts our operational readiness and effectiveness.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Can MINDEF provide an update on the recent steps taken to improve training safety whilst ensuring that our operational needs are not compromised?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman, you may take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As MINDEF and the SAF continue their relentless pursuit of safety and effectiveness, particularly in the domains of training realism, information dissemination and health monitoring, the pivotal role of technology in driving these advancements becomes increasingly apparent.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Harnessing the power of technological innovations holds the promise of not only enhancing training efficacy but also ensuring the safety and well-being of our personnel.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Could the Minister for Defence elaborate on additional plans MINDEF has in utilising technology to further enhance the safety of our NSmen?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The incorporation of "safety" into the SAF's core values in 2016 underscored the institution's commitment to achieving zero training fatalities while ensuring realistic training scenarios.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Could MINDEF provide an overview of the outcomes and learning points derived from the recent safety audits and reviews conducted within the SAF?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Additionally, an update on the work of the Inspector-General's Office, along with findings from safety audits conducted in the past years, would be greatly appreciated.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Chairman, the mental well-being of our National Servicemen (NSmen) is as crucial as their physical fitness.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Serving NS entails not only physical challenges but also mental and emotional stress, which can impact the overall well-being and performance.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Recognising the importance of mental resilience, it is essential to provide robust support systems and resources to address mental health concerns and promoting a culture of support within the military environment.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: In light of the increasing recognition of the importance of mental health in the overall well-being, what recent steps have MINDEF taken to enhance mental health support and resources for our NSmen?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: How are these initiatives tailored to address the unique challenges and stressors they face to ensure that they effective mental support?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It involves cultivating a resilient and balanced force that can withstand the rigours of duty and adapt to adversity in the complex dimensions of a modern conflict.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Interventions that emphasise optimism, resilience, well-being and proportionate behaviour should be incorporated early to empower our servicemen and women to navigate the challenges of their duties with an approach to allow them to not only endure but thrive.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The GAT is confidential and is an annual requirement for soldiers and is linked to the ArmyFit online training platform, which provides training based on the GAT results.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It has been taken by over one million soldiers and researchers have found that it appears to be a sound psychometric measure of competencies as well as leadership and character traits that are essential to army life.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This enhances unit cohesion, decision-making and overall mission success, and provides skills that will undoubtedly be helpful beyond their time in the Armed Forces.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Such assessments should not only be focusing on weaknesses or pathologies but instead, would also be focusing on identifying strengths that will increase resilience.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Shawn Huang, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As technology rapidly evolves, it is important for the Government to take the opportunity to redesign and streamline public services, ensuring that processes are easy to follow and are able to engage stakeholders effectively.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As citizens of a smart nation, we also understand first-hand the value of harnessing technology to transform the way we live and work.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This too can be applied to the NS experience.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I was happy to hear MINDEF's update that ground feedback on the automated make-up pay system has thus far been good.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: At the Committee of Supply debate last year, MINDEF updated that the first phase of the OneNS was rolled out to selected In-Camp Training units.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Intended as a replacement for the existing NS Portal, the key benefit of the OneNS app has the potential of centralising all NS-related services and transactions into a single mobile app, enhancing efficiency and ease of access.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I understand that the app is also able to anticipate and determine the unique needs of each serviceman and personalise digital services to ensure easy access to relevant information.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Compared to the challenges that some may have encountered in using the NS Portal, I hope that the OneNS app will go a long way in improving the NS experience for all.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Miss Rachel Ong, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Defence serves as a pillar of societal stability, safeguarding our freedoms and way of life.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, its importance is often only truly appreciated in its absence, leading to the tendency to take the presence of strong defence for granted.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Therefore, I would like to express my gratitude to our NSmen for their dedication to Singapore's national defence.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The commitment of our NSmen to balancing personal, professional and NS responsibilities during their reservist years is truly commendable.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Over time, MINDEF has made efforts to simplify processes and lessen administrative burdens for NSmen.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These initiatives include the automation of make-up pay claims and the digital distribution of NS Recognition benefits.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This development aims to provide a more user-friendly and convenient experience, eliminating the need for NSmen to visit multiple sites across Singapore and for services such as health screenings, annual fitness tests and equipment procurement.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As it has been five years since the groundbreaking ceremony, can MINDEF provide an update on the progress of this facility?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Our servicemen and women are the foundation of our defence force, and it is imperative that we prioritise their well-being by ensuring they have easy access to the healthcare services and resources that they need.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Last February marked the opening of the Kranji Regional Health Hub, the first of six regional health hubs aimed at providing comprehensive healthcare services to SAF camps in Singapore's north-western region.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These hubs are tailored to meet the specific healthcare needs of the units in surrounding camps.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I am encouraged to learn that the Health Hub offers an array of enhanced medical services, including dental, physiotherapy and mental well-being support, with unique features that enhance pandemic readiness.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The introduction of telehealth services to the region's camps also represents a step towards more convenient healthcare options for our servicemen and women.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Efforts to enhance the accessibility and quality of healthcare for our soldiers are crucial and must be sustained.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, NS is an obligation that every male Singaporean or second-generation Permanent Resident (PR) must fulfil.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, it is undeniably an opportunity cost that is disproportionately levied upon one segment of society.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Due to NS, Singaporean men begin their careers two years behind their female peers, first-generation PRs, new citizens and foreigners.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: NS poses a significant challenge for aspiring professional athletes, disrupting their training and competition during their peak performance years, and hindering their world-class aspirations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The current philosophy of giving NSFs an "allowance for basic upkeep" needs to be reviewed in view of the significant increase in cost of living and NSFs' opportunity costs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As a first step, the terminology should be changed from "NS allowance" to "NS salary", and it should attract CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This still would not be a market salary, but it will go some way to compensate NSFs for the opportunity cost of two years of service and help them contribute a little to their household income.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I must emphasise that this does not in any way diminish the ethos of NS – just because we pay our NSFs fairly does not mean their service is any less of a national duty.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: My cut is on SkillsFuture@NS, shortening time-to-work proficiency for NSmen.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: IPS noted respondents felt that, and I quote, "NS should include more non-military training.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This could be a result of the growing pressures for all to upskill and commit to lifelong learning, coupled with perceptions that NS involved some trade-offs to NSmen's education and career trajectories." Given the speed of technological innovation, a new NS-man with polytechnic education entering the workforce must now contend with fast-evolving industries and a steep learning curve.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: It is a tall order for a young person.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I wish to put forth three broad questions to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, the concept of Total Defence was first introduced in Singapore in 1984, recognising that defending Singapore required a whole-of-society approach.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At that time, the key pillars were military, civil, economic, social and psychological defence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In 2019, a sixth pillar, digital defence was added.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Although Total Defence involves everyone, generally, MINDEF has taken the lead on coordinating defence across all pillars.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Presently, two major armed conflicts are being fought – the Russia-Ukraine war in Europe and the Israel-Hamas conflict in the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Both conflicts have caused immense loss of human life and displaced millions of civilians.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Both conflicts have expanded also beyond the traditional battlefield and military domains.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These conflicts show that the modern warfare is total in nature, involving not only militaries, but the whole of society.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In both conflicts, we have seen how important it is for societies to be resilient and united in the face of adversity.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
